definition: A published set of principles that states how members of a profession should act toward the public, clients, and one another.
wrongs: A private price list that fixes the fees a consultant may charge for each technical task.
A compiler option that rejects source files which break a house style for names and comments.
A personal checklist an employee may ignore whenever a deadline is tight.
why: Professional bodies publish codes of ethics so members share duties such as honesty, competence, and regard for the public.
example: An engineer refuses to hide a known safety defect in a client report because the society's code requires honesty.
scenario: A client asks you to omit a known safety defect from a report so the product can ship. Which action fits a code of ethics?
scenarioAnswer: Refuse to hide the defect and record it honestly
scenarioWrongs: Omit the defect to keep the client relationship
Ship on time and delete the test notes
Sign the report and leave the decision to sales
scenarioWhy: A code of ethics requires honesty and regard for safety, so a known defect must not be concealed.

definition: Principles published by the Association for Computing Machinery that call for public good, honesty, fairness, privacy, and professional competence.
wrongs: A United Nations treaty that sets criminal penalties for every software bug in member states.
A vendor warranty that promises a full refund if an application fails a single test.
A university grading rubric used only to mark first-year programming labs.
why: The ACM Code is a widely used computing ethics code covering duties to the public and to the profession.
example: A developer cites the ACM principles when declining to build a feature designed to mislead users about fees.
scenario: You are asked to design a dark pattern that hides cancellation fees. Which ACM-aligned response is appropriate?
scenarioAnswer: Decline the feature because it deceives users
scenarioWrongs: Build it if the product manager signs the ticket
Build it but disable it in the demo build only
Add the pattern and mention it in an internal joke
scenarioWhy: The ACM Code requires honesty and avoidance of harm, so a feature meant to mislead users should be refused.

definition: Workplace or membership rules that set expected behaviour, including respect, compliance, and consequences for breaches.
wrongs: A scientific theory that predicts how fast a team will finish a software release.
A hardware manual that only lists the pin voltages of a microcontroller.
A marketing slogan used on the company website and business cards.
why: A code of conduct turns expected behaviour into rules people can follow and that the organisation can enforce.
example: After a staff member mocks a colleague in a client meeting, HR applies the code of conduct's respect rules.
scenario: A teammate shares a colleague's private photo in a project chat. Which document most directly forbids that behaviour?
scenarioAnswer: The workplace code of conduct
scenarioWrongs: The office coffee-machine warranty
The compiler's warning level settings
The building's floor-plan drawing
scenarioWhy: A code of conduct sets respectful behaviour and the consequences of harassing or humiliating colleagues.

definition: The duty to give weight to public safety and welfare when a decision could affect people beyond the employer or client.
wrongs: The duty to maximise the employer's profit even when users are put at known risk.
A requirement to publish every internal email on the company website each day.
A rule that only government employees, never private contractors, owe any care to users.
why: Computing codes treat the public good as a primary duty when systems can harm people outside the contract.
example: A contractor delays a launch and tells the regulator about a flaw that could expose patient records.
scenario: Shipping this week would raise revenue, but a flaw can leak patient records. Which duty should lead the decision?
scenarioAnswer: Protect the public from the data leak
scenarioWrongs: Protect the quarterly revenue target only
Hide the flaw until the next financial year
Let the sales team vote on the medical risk
scenarioWhy: Public-interest duty puts safety and welfare ahead of a purely commercial reason to ship a dangerous flaw.

definition: The knowledge, skill, and care required to perform a task to the standard expected of a qualified practitioner.
wrongs: The number of years someone has held a job title, regardless of the task at hand.
A promise that every graduate can legally certify any system in any specialism.
The speed at which a person answers chat messages during the working day.
why: Competence is about being able to do the specific work safely and correctly, not about title or confidence alone.
example: A web developer declines to sign off a medical-device design because that work is outside their competence.
scenario: You are asked to certify a safety-critical design you have never been trained to assess. Which response shows competence?
scenarioAnswer: Decline and refer the work to a qualified person
scenarioWrongs: Sign it because the deadline is tomorrow
Copy a certificate from a previous project
Ask an intern to approve it in your name
scenarioWhy: Professional competence means you do not claim or sign work you are not qualified to judge.

definition: An obligation to take reasonable care so that professional work does not cause foreseeable harm to clients or the public.
wrongs: A promise to guarantee profit for every client who buys a software product.
A duty to work unlimited unpaid hours whenever a manager requests it.
A rule that only applies after a court case has already been lost.
why: Duty of care is the legal and professional obligation to act as a reasonable practitioner would, so foreseeable harm is avoided.
example: Before go-live, an analyst insists on a backup test because a failed migration could wipe customer orders.
scenario: A rushed configuration could wipe customer orders, and a backup test would take one hour. Which action meets a duty of care?
scenarioAnswer: Run the backup test before go-live
scenarioWrongs: Skip the test to save the hour
Go live and hope users keep paper copies
Disable backups so the failure is faster
scenarioWhy: Duty of care requires reasonable steps against a foreseeable loss, such as testing the backup first.

definition: Honest and consistent adherence to professional standards, including refusing to misstate facts or hide material defects.
wrongs: Loyalty that requires you to lie whenever a supervisor prefers a simpler story.
A measure of how many programming languages appear on a CV.
The practice of agreeing with every client opinion to avoid conflict.
why: Integrity means the professional's statements and actions stay truthful and consistent with their duties.
example: A tester reports a failed acceptance test even though the project manager asks for a green status slide.
scenario: The status slide would look better if you marked a failed test as passed. Which response shows integrity?
scenarioAnswer: Report the test as failed
scenarioWrongs: Mark it passed and mention it after launch
Delete the test so there is no failure
Change the expected result to match the bug
scenarioWhy: Integrity requires an honest report of the test result even when a green slide would be more convenient.

definition: Being answerable for one's professional decisions, actions, and their consequences.
wrongs: The right to remain anonymous for every decision made in a paid role.
A rule that blame always moves to the most junior person on the team.
A financial metric equal to last year's profit divided by headcount.
why: Accountability means a named person can be asked to explain a decision and its results.
example: The engineer who approved a firewall change writes the incident note when that change causes an outage.
scenario: A change you approved causes an outage. Which response shows accountability?
scenarioAnswer: Own the decision and help write the incident facts
scenarioWrongs: Delete the approval record from the log
Blame an unnamed vendor with no evidence
Refuse to discuss it because the sprint ended
scenarioWhy: Accountability means the person who approved the change helps explain what happened and why.

definition: Disclosing suspected illegal, unsafe, or seriously unethical conduct to a person or body that can investigate it.
wrongs: Posting routine office complaints on a public social network for entertainment.
Leaking a client's design to a competitor in exchange for a job offer.
Reporting a colleague for using a different code editor from yours.
why: Whistleblowing is a disclosure of serious wrongdoing to someone who can act, not gossip or a personal grievance about taste.
example: After internal reports are ignored, an analyst tells the regulator that test results on a medical system were falsified.
scenario: Falsified safety tests were reported internally and ignored. Which next step is whistleblowing?
scenarioAnswer: Disclose the falsification to a body that can investigate
scenarioWrongs: Sell the test data to a competitor
Post jokes about the team on social media
Delete the evidence to avoid an argument
scenarioWhy: Whistleblowing means reporting serious wrongdoing to a proper investigating authority when internal correction has failed.

definition: A failure to take the care that a reasonable professional in the same situation would take, causing foreseeable loss.
wrongs: Any error in software, even when the developer followed accepted practice and warned of residual risk.
A deliberate decision to steal client funds for personal use.
A disagreement between two experts who both followed a recognised method.
why: Negligence is careless failure to meet the standard of a reasonable professional, not every mistake or a deliberate crime.
example: A consultant skips a standard backup check, and the client's database is lost during an upgrade.
scenario: A practitioner skips a standard check that peers always do, and the client loses data. Which label fits that failure?
scenarioAnswer: Negligence
scenarioWrongs: A reasonable difference of expert opinion
An unavoidable natural disaster
Proper care that still had a disclosed residual risk
scenarioWhy: Skipping a check that a reasonable practitioner would perform, with foreseeable loss, is negligence.

definition: The duty to protect non-public information and to disclose it only to people who are authorised to receive it.
wrongs: The duty to publish all project documents so that anyone on the internet can audit them.
A promise that information, once learned, may be freely reused in a personal blog.
A technical setting that encrypts disks but places no duty on the people who can read the data.
why: Confidentiality is a duty on people to limit disclosure of non-public information to those allowed to see it.
example: A support engineer refuses to read a customer's payroll file aloud when friends visit the office.
scenario: Friends visit the office and ask you to show a customer's payroll file. Which response keeps confidentiality?
scenarioAnswer: Refuse and keep the file closed
scenarioWrongs: Show the file because they promised not to tell
Email the file to your personal account to explain it later
Print a copy for them to read on the way out
scenarioWhy: Confidentiality allows disclosure only to authorised people, and visiting friends are not authorised.

definition: A contract that obliges one or both parties to keep specified information secret and to limit how it is used.
wrongs: A public press release that announces a product and invites journalists to share it.
A software feature that automatically posts status updates to social media.
A verbal joke between colleagues that no one writes down.
why: A non-disclosure agreement is a contract that creates a binding duty of secrecy about defined information.
example: Before a vendor demo, both firms sign an agreement that the prototype design must not be shared.
scenario: A journalist asks for details of a prototype covered by a signed secrecy contract. Which response fits that contract?
scenarioAnswer: Decline and protect the specified information
scenarioWrongs: Send the design files for a fair article
Describe the secret algorithm in full
Post the prototype video on a public channel
scenarioWhy: A non-disclosure agreement requires the signer to keep the specified information secret.

definition: The rule that sensitive information is shared only with people who require it to perform their current duties.
wrongs: The rule that every employee may browse every customer record in case it becomes useful later.
A requirement to copy the whole executive team on every password reset.
A practice of posting system credentials on a shared noticeboard.
why: Need-to-know limits access to people whose present duties require that information, which reduces exposure.
example: Payroll data for a misconduct case is given only to HR and the investigator, not to the whole department.
scenario: A developer wants the full payroll file out of curiosity while fixing a login bug. Which decision fits need-to-know?
scenarioAnswer: Deny access because the bug does not require payroll data
scenarioWrongs: Grant the whole file so they can browse freely
Email the file to the entire engineering list
Print it and leave it in the shared kitchen
scenarioWhy: Need-to-know grants sensitive data only when current duties require it, and curiosity is not a duty.

definition: Agreement given after a person understands what information will be collected, why, and the main consequences.
wrongs: A hidden default that opts people in because they once visited a website.
A manager's signature that approves a budget, with no data subject involved.
A pop-up that says continue, with no explanation of the data collected.
why: Consent is informed only when the person understands the collection, the purpose, and the main effects before agreeing.
example: A pilot app explains location tracking and retention, and staff tick agree before any tracking starts.
scenario: You want to track staff phones in a pilot. Which step is required for informed consent?
scenarioAnswer: Explain the tracking and get agreement before it starts
scenarioWrongs: Turn tracking on quietly and mention it at year end
Rely on a banner that only says continue
Ask the facilities manager to consent for everyone
scenarioWhy: Informed consent requires each person to understand the tracking and agree before collection begins.

definition: Collecting and keeping only the personal data that is adequate, relevant, and limited to a stated purpose.
wrongs: Copying every available field about a person so future unknown projects have spare data.
Deleting all records immediately, even those the law requires the business to keep.
Encrypting a database while still collecting every unrelated personal detail.
why: Data minimisation limits collection and retention to what the stated purpose actually needs.
example: A conference form asks for name and email only, after the team drops an unused question about home address.
scenario: A webinar only needs name and email, but the form also asks for home address and national ID. Which change fits data minimisation?
scenarioAnswer: Remove the address and ID fields
scenarioWrongs: Add date of birth in case marketing wants it later
Require a scan of a passport for a public webinar
Keep every extra field because storage is cheap
scenarioWhy: Data minimisation keeps only personal data needed for the webinar, which is name and email.

definition: Using personal data only for the purpose explained when it was collected, or for a compatible purpose the law allows.
wrongs: A rule that data collected for one campaign may be sold to any buyer without further thought.
A requirement to invent a new purpose after collection and apply it silently.
The practice of mixing staff health records into a sales mailing list.
why: Purpose limitation stops personal data collected for one stated reason being reused for an incompatible reason.
example: Emails gathered for a safety recall are not added to a marketing list for unrelated products.
scenario: Customers gave emails for a safety recall. Marketing wants those addresses for a new toy catalogue. Which decision fits purpose limitation?
scenarioAnswer: Do not use the recall list for the catalogue
scenarioWrongs: Send the catalogue because the addresses already exist
Sell the list to a partner for a fee
Merge the recall list into every future campaign
scenarioWhy: Purpose limitation keeps recall contacts for the recall, not for an unrelated marketing catalogue.

definition: A statement that tells people what personal data is collected, for what purpose, who receives it, and what rights they have.
wrongs: A secret internal memo that tells staff never to explain data uses to customers.
A copyright symbol placed in the footer of a website.
A firewall log that records blocked packets but is never shown to users.
why: A privacy notice is the explanation given to people so they know how their personal data will be used.
example: A signup page links to a notice describing the fields collected, the retention period, and how to request a copy.
scenario: Students will upload ID numbers to a placement portal. Which artefact should explain the collection, purpose, and their rights?
scenarioAnswer: A privacy notice
scenarioWrongs: A source-code header comment
A keyboard shortcut card
A blank non-disclosure agreement with no data explanation
scenarioWhy: A privacy notice is the statement that tells people what data is collected, why, and what rights they have.

definition: A security incident leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, or unauthorised disclosure of personal data.
wrongs: Any slow database query, even when no personal data is exposed or changed.
A planned backup that copies personal data to an authorised encrypted store.
A user updating their own password through the official reset page.
why: A personal data breach is an incident that compromises personal data, not every technical fault or authorised processing.
example: A spreadsheet of student phone numbers is emailed to the wrong external supplier, and the team logs a breach.
scenario: A file of student phone numbers is emailed to the wrong supplier. Which label should the team apply?
scenarioAnswer: Personal data breach
scenarioWrongs: Ordinary slow query
Authorised backup
Routine password reset by the student
scenarioWhy: Sending personal data to an unauthorised recipient is an unauthorised disclosure, which is a personal data breach.

definition: Legal rights in creations of the mind, such as software, writing, designs, and brands, that can restrict unauthorised use.
wrongs: The physical computers and desks owned by an IT department.
A person's salary grade and annual leave balance.
The electricity consumed by a data centre in one month.
why: Intellectual property covers legal rights in intangible creations, not the organisation's physical assets or payroll data.
example: A startup treats its source code, logo, and user manual as intellectual property when negotiating an investment.
scenario: An investor asks what intangible creations the firm can legally protect. Which set is intellectual property?
scenarioAnswer: The source code, logo, and user manual
scenarioWrongs: The office chairs and server racks
The monthly electricity bill
The staff leave balances
scenarioWhy: Intellectual property rights attach to creations such as code, brands, and writing, not to furniture or utility bills.

definition: A legal right that controls copying, sharing, and adaptation of an original work such as code, text, images, or music.
wrongs: A right that protects only inventions with a new technical effect, such as a machine.
A registry entry that protects a brand name and logo from confusing use by rivals.
A secret recipe that is protected only while nobody else discovers it independently.
why: Copyright arises in original expressive works and restricts copying and adaptation; it is not a patent, trademark, or trade secret.
example: A student who copies a classmate's essay into an assignment infringes copyright as well as academic rules.
scenario: You want to paste a photographer's image into a commercial app without permission. Which right is most directly involved?
scenarioAnswer: Copyright in the photograph
scenarioWrongs: A patent on the camera's brand name
A trade secret in the public pixel colours
A trademark on the idea of taking photos
scenarioWhy: A photograph is an original work protected by copyright, so commercial copying needs permission or a legal exception.

definition: A legal permission that states whether, and on what conditions, a person may use, copy, or modify a software product.
wrongs: A hardware receipt that proves the company paid for a laptop.
A style guide that only describes bracket placement in source code.
An employment badge that opens the office door.
why: A software licence is the legal permission and its conditions, separate from a purchase receipt or a coding style.
example: An IT manager checks that a library's licence allows commercial distribution before shipping it inside a product.
scenario: A library is free to download, but the team wants to ship it inside a paid product. Which document decides whether that is allowed?
scenarioAnswer: The software licence
scenarioWrongs: The laptop purchase receipt
The office door-badge policy
The team's bracket style guide
scenarioWhy: The software licence states the conditions on use, copying, and distribution, including inside a commercial product.

definition: A licence that allows others to use, study, modify, and share the source code, subject to the conditions it states.
wrongs: A promise that every open-source program has no conditions and may never require attribution.
A licence that withholds source code and forbids modification by customers.
A government grant that pays a vendor to keep a program closed.
why: Open-source licences grant use, study, modification, and sharing, while still imposing stated conditions.
example: A team adopts a library after confirming its open-source licence lets them read, change, and redistribute the code.
scenario: A student claims a project is open source but refuses to let anyone see or change the source. Which conclusion is sound?
scenarioAnswer: It does not meet an open-source licence
scenarioWrongs: Secrecy of the source is required for open source
Open source forbids any conditions at all
Open source means the author must work unpaid forever
scenarioWhy: An open-source licence must allow others to use, study, modify, and share the source code.

definition: A licence condition that requires modified versions, when distributed, to stay under the same or a compatible share-alike licence.
wrongs: A rule that all software on earth must be given away with no licence text.
A permissive notice that allows a modified program to be relicensed as fully closed with no share-alike duty.
A trademark that stops rivals using a product name.
why: Copyleft is the share-alike condition in some open-source licences, not a ban on all conditions and not a permissive waiver.
example: A company that distributes a modified copyleft tool also publishes its changes under a compatible share-alike licence.
scenario: You distribute a modified program that carries a share-alike condition. Which obligation does copyleft impose?
scenarioAnswer: Distribute your modifications under a compatible share-alike licence
scenarioWrongs: Keep the modified source closed and drop the licence
Register the algorithm as a trademark
Charge no price and delete all copyright notices
scenarioWhy: Copyleft requires distributed modifications to remain under the same or a compatible share-alike licence.

definition: A time-limited exclusive right, granted by a government, to stop others exploiting an invention that meets the legal tests.
wrongs: An automatic right in every sentence you type, with no application to the state.
A secret that is protected only for as long as you successfully hide it.
A logo registration that stops confusing use of a brand name.
why: A patent is a granted, time-limited exclusive right in an invention, unlike automatic copyright or a hidden trade secret.
example: A firm files a patent application for a new compression method and, once granted, can stop unlicensed use for a limited term.
scenario: A rival is selling a device that copies your granted invention. Which right is designed for that situation?
scenarioAnswer: A patent
scenarioWrongs: A hidden trade secret you already published in full
A font copyright in the user manual only
A domain-name renewal receipt
scenarioWhy: A granted patent is the time-limited right used to stop others exploiting a qualifying invention.

definition: A sign, such as a name or logo, that identifies the source of goods or services and is protected against confusing use.
wrongs: The exclusive right to a technical invention for a fixed term after a patent grant.
The right to stop all criticism of a company in a newspaper review.
Ownership of every English word that appears in a product manual.
why: A trademark identifies commercial source and stops confusing use of that sign; it does not own ordinary language or inventions.
example: A startup changes its app icon after a lawyer warns that the icon is confusingly similar to a registered brand.
scenario: Your new logo is confusingly similar to a rival's registered brand for the same service. Which right have you most likely collided with?
scenarioAnswer: Their trademark
scenarioWrongs: Their patent on the English alphabet
Their copyright in the idea of having customers
Their trade secret in a public logo
scenarioWhy: A trademark protects a distinctive sign of origin against confusing use on similar goods or services.

definition: Confidential business information that has value because it is not generally known and is subject to reasonable secrecy measures.
wrongs: Information published in a patent specification, which is available to the public.
A famous logo printed on every product box.
A method taught in an open textbook and used by the whole industry.
why: A trade secret stays protected only while it is secret, valuable, and guarded by reasonable steps.
example: A company stores its ranking formula in a restricted repository and forbids staff from discussing it outside the team.
scenario: You are considering publishing a valuable formula that rivals do not know. Which protection would publication destroy?
scenarioAnswer: Trade secret protection
scenarioWrongs: A granted patent's remaining term
The copyright in a novel you did not publish
A trademark registration for your public logo
scenarioWhy: Trade-secret protection depends on secrecy, so publishing the formula ends that protection.

definition: The usual rule that copyright in work an employee creates as part of the job belongs to the employer, unless a contract says otherwise.
wrongs: A rule that every program a student writes at home on a weekend automatically belongs to a future employer.
A rule that freelancers always lose copyright even when the contract assigns it to them.
A rule that employers own the employee's personal photos and private diaries.
why: In ordinary employment, work created in the course of the job is owned by the employer unless the contract allocates it differently.
example: A developer writes a scheduling module during paid hours, and the employment contract states the company owns that code.
scenario: You wrote a module as part of your paid duties, and the contract gives copyright to the company. Who owns that code?
scenarioAnswer: The employer
scenarioWrongs: You alone, because you typed it
The first customer who sees the screen
A classmate who suggested a variable name
scenarioWhy: Work created as part of the job is ordinarily owned by the employer when the contract says so.

definition: Giving clear credit to the creator or source when you reuse their work, as required by academic rules or the licence.
wrongs: Removing the author's name so the work looks original.
Paying a fee that automatically cancels any need to name a source the licence still requires.
Changing the licence text so that credit clauses disappear.
why: Attribution is the credit given to the source, and many academic rules and licences still require it when work is reused.
example: A report that reuses a diagram keeps the creator's name and the licence notice under the figure.
scenario: A licence lets you reuse a diagram if you credit the creator. You include the diagram in a client report. Which step is still required?
scenarioAnswer: Keep the creator's name and required notice
scenarioWrongs: Remove the name so the diagram looks original
Replace the notice with your company logo only
Claim you drew it because you resized it
scenarioWhy: Attribution means giving the credit the licence or academic rule still requires when the work is reused.

definition: Presenting another person's words, code, or ideas as your own without appropriate credit.
wrongs: Quoting a source with quotation marks and a full citation.
Writing an original analysis that cites every borrowed idea.
Using a common fact, such as the number of days in a week, with no citation.
why: Plagiarism is passing off someone else's work or ideas as yours, which proper quotation and citation avoid.
example: A student pastes a blog's explanation of encryption into an essay and does not cite the blog.
scenario: You paste a blog's paragraph into your essay and do not cite it. Which description fits that submission?
scenarioAnswer: Plagiarism
scenarioWrongs: A properly cited quotation
An original argument with full references
Use of a commonplace fact such as the days in a week
scenarioWhy: Using someone else's words as your own without credit is plagiarism.

definition: The status of a work that is no longer protected by copyright, or whose owner has waived those rights, so reuse no longer needs permission.
wrongs: Any file that can be downloaded without creating an account.
A work that is free of charge but still all rights reserved.
A work you may copy only inside a classroom and not elsewhere.
why: Public domain means copyright no longer restricts reuse, which is different from merely being free to view or download.
example: A publisher reprints a nineteenth-century manual whose copyright has expired, without asking permission.
scenario: A manual's copyright has expired. Which reuse does public-domain status allow?
scenarioAnswer: Reprint it without asking permission
scenarioWrongs: Treat a free download with all rights reserved as automatically reusable
Ignore a separate trademark on the modern publisher's logo
Assume every unpaid website article is unprotected
scenarioWhy: Once copyright has expired, permission is no longer required to copy the work, which is public-domain status.

definition: A situation in which a personal, financial, or family interest could improperly influence a professional decision.
wrongs: Any disagreement between two colleagues about a technical design.
A requirement to hold shares in every supplier the company uses.
The ordinary duty to follow a documented architecture standard.
why: A conflict of interest exists when a personal stake could bias a decision the professional is trusted to make impartially.
example: An evaluator declares that their sibling owns a bidding firm and steps out of that vendor decision.
scenario: You are scoring bids, and your sibling owns one bidder. Which response addresses the conflict of interest?
scenarioAnswer: Declare it and step out of that decision
scenarioWrongs: Score your sibling's bid highest and say nothing
Ask your sibling what score they prefer
Delete the other bids so the choice is simple
scenarioWhy: A family financial interest can bias the scoring, so the conflict must be declared and the person should step aside.

definition: Rules that state when staff may accept gifts or hospitality and when they must declare or refuse them.
wrongs: A rule that expensive gifts from bidders must be accepted so the firm looks polite.
A ban on ever thanking a colleague for covering a shift.
A requirement to publish staff home addresses when a gift arrives.
why: Gift and hospitality rules manage influence by setting when offers may be kept, must be declared, or must be refused.
example: A buyer refuses match tickets from a bidder during a live tender because the policy forbids that hospitality.
scenario: During a live tender, a bidder offers you expensive match tickets. The policy forbids hospitality from bidders. Which action is right?
scenarioAnswer: Refuse the tickets and record the offer
scenarioWrongs: Accept them and score that bidder higher
Accept them if you tell no one
Ask for cash of the same value instead
scenarioWhy: The gift and hospitality policy exists to stop bidders influencing a live decision with valuable offers.

definition: Offering, giving, or accepting something of value to improperly influence a decision or obtain an unfair advantage.
wrongs: Paying a published official fee for a licence that everyone in the queue must pay.
Giving a modest declared thank-you gift that policy expressly allows after a contract ends.
Negotiating a lower price in an open and documented procurement.
why: Bribery is a benefit given or taken to distort a decision, unlike a published fee or an open commercial negotiation.
example: A supplier offers a buyer cash to ignore a failed security test, and the buyer reports the offer.
scenario: A supplier offers you cash to ignore a failed security test. Which description fits the offer?
scenarioAnswer: Bribery
scenarioWrongs: A published fee everyone must pay
An open price negotiation
A declared gift that policy allows after the contract
scenarioWhy: Cash offered to ignore a failed test is a benefit meant to improperly influence a professional decision.

definition: Paid work outside the main job that may compete with the employer or impair the employee's duties.
wrongs: Unpaid volunteering that the employer has approved and that does not affect work.
Attending a mandatory training course during paid hours.
Taking contractual annual leave to rest.
why: Moonlighting is outside paid work that can create competition, fatigue, or a conflict with the main employer.
example: A developer takes weekend paid work for a direct competitor and uses sleep time so weekday performance drops.
scenario: Your contract requires you to declare outside paid work. You start a paid weekend job for a direct competitor. Which step is required?
scenarioAnswer: Declare the outside work before continuing
scenarioWrongs: Use the employer's customer list to help the weekend job
Hide it because it happens on Saturday
Do the competitor's work on the office laptop in secret
scenarioWhy: Moonlighting for a competitor can conflict with the employer, and the contract requires it to be declared.

definition: Stepping aside from a decision or review because a personal interest would undermine impartiality.
wrongs: Staying in the decision and promising yourself you will be fair.
Reporting a crime to an external authority after internal reports fail.
Resigning from the profession permanently because of one project delay.
why: Recusal removes the person from the specific decision their interest could bias.
example: A reviewer leaves the room while the panel scores a proposal from a company where they hold shares.
scenario: You hold shares in a firm whose proposal you were asked to score. Which action is recusal?
scenarioAnswer: Step out of scoring that proposal
scenarioWrongs: Stay and award it the top score quietly
Publish the proposal on social media
Resign from your whole career on the spot
scenarioWhy: Recusal means leaving the particular decision that your shareholding could bias.

definition: Clear, respectful, and purposeful exchange of information suited to the audience and the workplace context.
wrongs: Using slang, insults, and unexplained jargon so that only close friends can follow.
Sending every document as a blank attachment with no message.
Speaking only in private jokes during a client incident review.
why: Professional communication is judged by clarity, respect, and fit to the audience and purpose.
example: During an outage, an analyst sends the client a short update in plain language with the next check time.
scenario: A client who is not a programmer asks for an outage update. Which message is professional communication?
scenarioAnswer: A short plain-language note with the impact and next update time
scenarioWrongs: A string of unexplained error codes and insults
A blank email with no text
A private joke sent only to your friends
scenarioWhy: Professional communication gives the audience a clear, respectful message they can act on.

definition: A concise record of attendees, decisions, action owners, and deadlines from a meeting.
wrongs: A word-for-word transcript of every joke and side conversation.
A slide that only shows the company's logo.
A personal diary entry that no attendee is allowed to see.
why: Minutes exist so people who were present or absent can see what was decided and who must act.
example: After a design meeting, the note lists three decisions, the owner of each action, and the due dates.
scenario: Several people missed the design meeting and need to know what was decided. Which record should be circulated?
scenarioAnswer: Meeting minutes with decisions, owners, and dates
scenarioWrongs: A private joke from the chat channel
An empty slide with only the logo
A full audio file of unrelated small talk and nothing else
scenarioWhy: Minutes record attendees, decisions, owners, and deadlines so absent people can follow the outcome.

definition: A periodic update that states progress, issues, risks, and the next actions on a piece of work.
wrongs: A final contract that sets salary and notice terms.
A one-line claim that everything is fine, with no progress or issues.
A raw dump of every keystroke logged on a laptop.
why: A status report is a regular picture of progress, problems, and next steps, not a contract or an empty reassurance.
example: Each Friday a project lead emails what was finished, one slipping task, and the action planned for Monday.
scenario: Your manager asks for this week's picture of a task that has slipped. Which content belongs in the status report?
scenarioAnswer: Progress, the slip, the risk, and the next action
scenarioWrongs: Only the word fine
The employment contract
A keystroke log from your laptop
scenarioWhy: A status report tells the reader progress, issues, risks, and what will be done next.

definition: Raising an unresolved professional issue to the next person who has authority to act on it.
wrongs: Posting the issue on a public social network before telling anyone at work.
Ignoring the issue until the contract ends.
Asking an uninvolved friend outside the organisation to decide company policy.
why: Escalation moves an issue up the agreed path to someone empowered to resolve it.
example: When a supplier misses a safety fix, the engineer informs the project sponsor after the supplier's manager does not respond.
scenario: A supplier has ignored a safety fix, and their manager will not respond. Which step is proper escalation?
scenarioAnswer: Raise it with the sponsor who can act
scenarioWrongs: Post the contract fight on public social media first
Wait silently until the warranty expires
Ask an unrelated friend to set company policy
scenarioWhy: Escalation takes the unresolved safety issue to the next person with authority to act.

definition: Workplace rules that define permitted and forbidden use of computers, accounts, networks, and data.
wrongs: A guide to the best restaurants near the office.
A law that bans all personal phone calls in an entire country.
A hardware schematic for a printer power supply.
why: An acceptable use policy tells staff what they may and may not do with organisational systems and data.
example: The policy forbids using a work account to run a private online shop or to share passwords.
scenario: You want to run a private online shop from your work email and server. The policy forbids personal commercial use. Which action complies?
scenarioAnswer: Do not use work systems for the shop
scenarioWrongs: Use the work server if you do it after 6 p.m.
Share your work password with a friend who will run the shop
Store customer card numbers in the team chat
scenarioWhy: An acceptable use policy defines forbidden uses of work systems, including a private business.

definition: A legal agreement that sets the role, pay, hours, duties, and main conditions of a job.
wrongs: A weekly status email about project tasks.
A canteen menu for the staff restaurant.
A software licence for a drawing tool.
why: An employment contract is the legal agreement of the job's core terms, not a project update or a tool licence.
example: Before starting, a graduate reads the contract's clauses on hours, pay, confidentiality, and intellectual property.
scenario: You need the agreed hours, pay, and confidentiality duties of your new job. Which document states those terms?
scenarioAnswer: The employment contract
scenarioWrongs: The canteen menu
This week's status email
The drawing tool's licence file
scenarioWhy: The employment contract is the agreement that sets role, pay, hours, duties, and main conditions.

definition: An initial period of employment used to assess suitability, often with shorter notice than after the post is confirmed.
wrongs: A permanent ban on training until the employee has worked for ten years.
A criminal sentence served outside the workplace.
The warranty period on a purchased laptop.
why: Probation is an early employment stage for assessing fit, often with different notice rules from a confirmed post.
example: During the first three months, a new analyst has fortnightly reviews and a shorter notice period than confirmed staff.
scenario: A new hire is in the first three months, with extra reviews and shorter notice, before the post is confirmed. Which term applies?
scenarioAnswer: Probation period
scenarioWrongs: Laptop warranty
A criminal sentence
A ten-year training ban
scenarioWhy: Probation is the opening period used to assess a new employee, often with shorter notice.

definition: Unwanted conduct that violates a person's dignity or creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive working environment.
wrongs: A polite one-off request to correct an error in a report.
Allocating work fairly according to a published rota.
Giving evidence-based feedback on a missed deadline in private.
why: Harassment is unwanted conduct that attacks dignity or creates a hostile environment, not ordinary management of work.
example: Repeated jokes about a colleague's accent continue after they ask for them to stop, and they report the conduct.
scenario: A colleague keeps mocking another's accent after being asked to stop, and the person feels the office is hostile. Which label fits?
scenarioAnswer: Workplace harassment
scenarioWrongs: A single polite correction of a report
Fair allocation on a published rota
Private feedback about a missed deadline
scenarioWhy: Repeated unwanted mockery that creates a hostile environment is workplace harassment.

definition: Treating a person less favourably at work because of a protected characteristic, rather than because of job requirements.
wrongs: Rejecting an applicant who lacks a skill the job genuinely requires.
Promoting the candidate with the stronger evidenced performance.
Providing the same safety training to every new starter.
why: Unlawful discrimination is less favourable treatment because of a protected characteristic, not a decision based on real job needs.
example: A manager refuses an interview to qualified applicants solely because of their religion, and HR treats it as discrimination.
scenario: Qualified applicants are refused interviews solely because of their religion. Which description fits that decision?
scenarioAnswer: Unlawful discrimination
scenarioWrongs: A fair rejection for a missing essential skill
Promotion based on stronger evidence
Giving every starter the same safety training
scenarioWhy: Refusing qualified people solely because of religion is less favourable treatment based on a protected characteristic.

definition: A practical change to equipment, duties, or the workplace that removes a substantial disadvantage for a disabled worker, where the change is reasonable.
wrongs: Lowering a safety-critical competence standard so that an unqualified person can sign off hazards.
A cash bonus paid to every employee regardless of need.
A refusal to consider any change once a person discloses a disability.
why: A reasonable adjustment changes the work context to remove a disadvantage, without pretending that unsafe incompetence is acceptable.
example: An employer provides screen-reader compatible tools so a blind analyst can do the same analysis as colleagues.
scenario: A blind analyst can do the role if the tools work with a screen reader. Which response is a reasonable adjustment?
scenarioAnswer: Provide screen-reader compatible tools
scenarioWrongs: Refuse any change after the disability is disclosed
Drop all safety checks for the whole team
Pay an unrelated bonus to every employee instead
scenarioWhy: A reasonable adjustment is a practical change, such as compatible tools, that removes a disadvantage for the worker.

definition: The shared obligation of employer and worker to reduce foreseeable risks of injury or ill health at work.
wrongs: A duty that falls only on visitors, never on the employer or the staff.
A promise that no workplace can ever contain any hazard.
A rule that forbids reporting hazards because it slows production.
why: Health and safety law and practice require both employer and worker to take reasonable steps against foreseeable harm.
example: A technician reports a trailing cable in a walkway, and the supervisor gets it taped down the same morning.
scenario: You notice a trailing cable across a busy walkway. Which action meets a worker's health and safety duty?
scenarioAnswer: Report it and help make the walkway safe
scenarioWrongs: Step over it and tell nobody
Cover the cable with a coat and leave it
Wait for a visitor to trip so there is proof
scenarioWhy: Workers share a duty to reduce foreseeable harm, so a trip hazard should be reported and controlled.

definition: A formal process for an employee to raise a workplace complaint and have it investigated and answered.
wrongs: The process a company uses to discipline an employee for misconduct.
A customer refund process for faulty goods.
A method for estimating how long a coding task will take.
why: A grievance procedure is the employee's formal route to have a workplace complaint heard and answered.
example: An analyst submits a written grievance about bullying, and HR investigates and gives a written outcome.
scenario: You have a serious unresolved complaint about bullying and want it formally investigated. Which process should you use?
scenarioAnswer: The grievance procedure
scenarioWrongs: The customer refund process
A task-estimation method
A public product review site
scenarioWhy: The grievance procedure is the formal route for an employee complaint to be investigated and answered.

definition: A formal process an employer follows before imposing a sanction for alleged misconduct or poor performance.
wrongs: The route an employee uses to complain about how they have been treated.
A celebration for meeting a sales target.
A backup schedule for the file server.
why: A disciplinary procedure is the employer's formal path for dealing with alleged misconduct or performance problems.
example: Before issuing a warning for repeated unauthorised access, HR sets out the allegation and lets the employee respond.
scenario: An employer believes an employee repeatedly misused access and may issue a warning. Which process should it follow first?
scenarioAnswer: The disciplinary procedure
scenarioWrongs: The employee grievance route as if the employer were complaining
A sales celebration
The server backup schedule
scenarioWhy: Disciplinary procedure is the formal process used before a sanction for alleged misconduct.

definition: Planned learning after qualification that keeps a practitioner's knowledge and skills current and relevant.
wrongs: A one-time school certificate that removes any later need to learn.
Repeating the same outdated course title on a CV without doing the learning.
A holiday taken to rest, with no learning aim.
why: Continuing professional development is ongoing, planned learning so practice stays current after formal qualification.
example: Each year a security engineer completes a course on current incident-response practice and applies it at work.
scenario: Your degree is five years old and a core tool has changed. Which activity is continuing professional development?
scenarioAnswer: Planned learning on the current tool and practice
scenarioWrongs: Listing an old course you did not attend
Assuming the degree removed any need to learn
Taking leave with no learning purpose
scenarioWhy: Continuing professional development is planned learning that updates skills after qualification.

definition: A log of learning activities and outcomes used as evidence that a professional has maintained their competence.
wrongs: A password list for work systems.
A timesheet that only records hours in the office.
A marketing brochure about a training vendor.
why: A CPD record is the evidence log of what was learned and what changed in practice, not a timesheet or a password store.
example: An engineer keeps a log of a cloud course, the date, and how it changed the way backups are designed.
scenario: A professional body asks for evidence of learning this year. Which item is a CPD record?
scenarioAnswer: A log of courses, dates, and how practice changed
scenarioWrongs: A list of system passwords
A timesheet of office hours only
A vendor's marketing brochure
scenarioWhy: A CPD record logs learning activities and outcomes as evidence that competence is being maintained.
